subtitle: The whole book in one newsroom: fold, unfold, connect, present
words.intro: A German newsroom in the last hour before the deadline. One story is too long, and one is too dry. Every word on these pages comes down to one question: can this be said shorter, or more honestly?

grammar[0].fact: Since 2006 the German spelling reform has been fully in force, after years of court cases, state votes and newspapers that refused to go along. Some writers still use the old rules. document.intro: A real masthead panel in a technical journal from East Germany. Every German paper by law must have an *Impressum*: who’s responsible. It’s a compact list, full of abbreviations, and it even says who’s allowed to reprint it.
document.fact: The law that requires an Impressum still holds, and it also binds every German website. Its purpose is simple: for every sentence, someone can be held to account. Note *Lizenznummer* here: in East Germany, you needed a licence to print.

reading.title: Andruck
reading.intro: Half past nine at the local paper, half an hour to press. Vroni has a story about the new bench law, and it’s twelve lines too long. The new proofreader has started this week: Herr Doktor Brummer, whom you may remember. He’s reading over her shoulder. He has a red pen, and it’s his wife’s.
reading.fact: The word *Andruck* is the moment the paper goes to press. Germany has been printing since Gutenberg, in Mainz, and the country’s editors have strong views on what happens at that hour. Press freedom is written into Article 5 of the Basic Law, and *Eine Zensur findet nicht statt* is a sentence every journalist can quote: censorship does not take place.
